story.headline: A report of a US–Iran peace framework knocked oil off a five-month high and pushed the dollar to a three-week low. The pound led the day, near $1.34 after strong UK jobs data.

reads.policy: The Fed's December hike stayed almost fully priced even as oil fell, so the US rate story held. Canada, New Zealand and Britain are still expected to hike first, and a hawkish Bank of England speaker backed the pound's case. Currencies whose banks are about to act keep the rate edge.
reads.growth: US housing is clearly weakening under high mortgage rates, which argues for a slower Fed and weighs a little on the dollar. German investors turned gloomier on high energy costs. Britain's job market still looks firm.
reads.inflation: Energy is still the main source of inflation pressure, and today's oil drop was the first hint of relief. A Bank of England policymaker said pay growth has stopped cooling at too high a level. Wednesday's UK and New Zealand inflation reports are the next tests for rate bets.
reads.risk: Hope for US–Iran diplomacy calmed markets: stocks rose, oil fell and the dollar slipped. But nothing is confirmed, a diplomat said a deal is not close, and attacks around Saudi Arabia continue. Safe havens lost a little of their lift; the franc still holds firm against the euro on French worries.
reads.tot: Oil swung from a five-month high to a loss on talk of diplomacy, though Gulf shipping is still badly disrupted. Cheaper oil helps importers like Japan and the euro area. Canada's currency gained anyway, because its rate story now matters more than the oil price.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds are betting most heavily against the Canadian dollar, and the loonie has now risen to a four-week high, which leaves those bets exposed. They also bet against the kiwi ahead of a likely hike. In the yen and the Aussie, hedge funds and long-term investors disagree.
reads.fiscal: France pushed its budget revenue vote back a week, so the risk to French bonds lingers without a verdict. Britain's 10-year bond sale went well, a calm read on UK debt before next week's budget. Moody's review of France on Friday is the next test for the euro.

fed.summary: The Fed is expected to hold in October and is now seen as nearly certain to hike in December. The dollar slipped today on lower oil, not on any change in the Fed outlook.
fed.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike very likely (about 9 in 10).
fed.why: Inflation is running hot and oil keeps it that way. Weak housing argues for caution, but short-term rates barely moved on it.
fed.watch: The Fed is in its quiet period until the October 28 decision. Until then, oil, US–Iran headlines and US yields set the tone.

boc.summary: Markets still expect the Bank of Canada to hike on October 28 after Macklem's oil warning. That, plus Alberta voting to stay in Canada, lifted the loonie to a four-week high.
boc.why: Macklem said the bank will raise its inflation forecast sharply and must act on where inflation is heading. Several big Canadian banks now call a hike.
boc.watch: Canada's retail sales later this week, oil prices, and whether any BoC official pushes back on hike bets before October 28.

rbnz.summary: Markets lean firmly toward an RBNZ hike on October 28. A firm dairy auction helped a little, but Wednesday's inflation report has to back the hike.
rbnz.why: Strong business activity, firmer dairy prices and the bank's own signal that rates are more likely to go up drive the hike bets. A wide trade gap is the main argument for waiting.
rbnz.watch: New Zealand's inflation report at 4:45 PM CT Wednesday. A clearly soft number would put a hold back on the table.

ecb.summary: The ECB is expected to hold in October and lean toward a December hike. France's budget fight drags on, but cheaper oil gave the euro some relief today.
ecb.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike likely.
ecb.why: Inflation is near a three-year high and factory prices are still rising, so a December hike stays the base case. Weaker investor morale and French bond stress are the worries.
ecb.watch: Lagarde on Wednesday, Moody's review of France on Friday, and France's budget vote, now on October 27.

boj.summary: The BoJ is signalling more hikes, most likely in December. The yen firmed a little today on strong bond demand and lower US yields, but the rate gap still keeps it weak.
boj.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike likely.
boj.why: Ueda said underlying inflation is close to the 2% goal, and record demand at a long-bond sale eased debt worries. But inflation is still below the bank's own forecast, so there is no rush.
boj.watch: Japan's trade figures tonight, the inflation report on Friday and the bank's new forecasts on October 30.

rba.summary: The RBA hints rates may not be high enough yet, keeping a November hike possible. The Aussie is back at 70 US cents on a softer dollar and better risk mood.
rba.priced: November: hike about 1 in 3; December: a coin flip.
rba.why: Kent said the neutral rate may be rising and inflation is stuck. He also said the job market is loosening faster than expected.
rba.watch: Deputy Governor Hauser speaks at 5:30 PM CT tonight, then Australia's quarterly inflation report on October 28.

boe.summary: The Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates on November 5. Strong jobs data and a hawkish speech from Greene pushed the pound to a five-week high.
boe.priced: November 5: hike almost fully expected; December an open question.
boe.why: Unemployment fell and pay growth edged up. Greene said wage growth has stopped cooling at a level too high for 2% inflation.
boe.watch: UK inflation at 1 AM CT Wednesday and Bailey's speech that morning. A hot number would bring a December hike into play.

snb.summary: The SNB holds at zero and could cut in December because Swiss inflation is very low. The franc is near its strongest against the euro in three months, close to where the SNB has pushed back before.
snb.priced: Holding at 0%; a December cut is possible.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is very soft, so the bank has no reason to tighten. The franc's strength comes from French debt worries and Gulf risk, not Swiss news.
snb.watch: Thursday's write-up of the SNB's last meeting, and whether the bank signals it will act against a stronger franc.
